column4: The section's wording “no food except” is repeated here as “ولا طعام إلا من غسلين”; a second Hell-food sharpens the image of an exception that cannot be ordinary nourishment.
The section cites Zaqqūm eaten until bellies are filled; this verse makes fullness bodily but leaves open the section's distinction between filling and nourishing.
The section's Zaqqūm comparison is made explicit by “فمالئون منها البطون”: bellies fill, while the section says its food still does not fatten or remove hunger.
The section's word طعام names the failed meal; here Zaqqūm is “طعام الأثيم,” making the food itself the sinners' punishment.
The section's food does not satisfy; this “طعاما ذا غصة” instead lodges in the throat, presenting eating that brings neither comfort nor relief.
The section says no food except ضريع; here the corresponding thirst scene has no drink except “حميمًا وغساقًا,” a painful exception rather than relief.
The section's food “does not relieve hunger” (root غ ن ي as named there); “ولا يغني من اللهب” uses the same failure-formula for shade that cannot protect from the flame.
The section quotes this continuation of the ghislin scene: “لا يأكله إلا الخاطئون” identifies who must eat the exceptional food.
The section quotes the preceding “ليس له ... حميم” before the food exception; the absence of a close companion makes the deprivation social as well as alimentary.
The section labels جوع as the hunger that food fails to remove; this verse says God “أطعمهم من جوع,” the direct opposite, and pairs relief from hunger with safety from fear.
The section's named root ج و ع appears in “ألا تجوع فيها”: the Garden is defined by absence of hunger, reversing the food that cannot satisfy.
The section describes food that cannot feed and a secondary dictionary sense of ضريع as a thin drink; Abraham names God as the one who “يطعمني ويسقين,” supplying both.
The section's word طعام fails precisely at hunger; “إطعام في يوم ذي مسغبة” is the human act of giving food when hunger is acute.
The section stages hunger despite an available but useless food; this town first receives abundant provision, then is made to taste “الجوع والخوف” after ingratitude.
The section's word طعام is reconsidered in “فلينظر الإنسان إلى طعامه”; the following verses show food as a provision made to sustain life, unlike ضريع.
The section's quoted ghislin passage is preceded by “ولا يحض على طعام المسكين”; this context links the punished person's deprivation to his failure to urge feeding the poor.
The section's food scene is for the punished; this confession, “ولم نك نطعم المسكين,” connects punishment to refusing to feed the needy.
The section's word طعام occurs in the Qur'anic rebuke “ولا تحاضون على طعام المسكين”; it makes the opposite of nourishing food a social refusal to encourage feeding.
The section's food cannot end hunger; this rebuke of the denier names failure to urge “طعام المسكين,” a human refusal to answer hunger.
The section gives food that cannot nourish; this righteous scene has people “يطعمون الطعام” to the needy, orphan, and captive, turning food into actual care.
The section's failed meal is set against the previous verse's feeding; this neighbor states the givers seek God's face rather than repayment or thanks.
The section's image of unrelieved hunger is answered by 90:14's feeding on a day of hunger; this neighbor specifies the recipient as a related orphan.
Continuing 90:14's food given on a hungry day, this verse names a poor person in dust, showing who receives real relief.
After 20:118's Garden promise of no hunger, this neighbor adds no thirst there; it completes the reversal of food and drink that fail to relieve need.
The section's dry plant cannot nourish; this verse begins the provision sequence after 80:24 by describing water poured down for food to grow.
The section names a dried plant; this neighbor describes earth split open in the productive chain that leads to the food listed next.
The section's “no food except” is contrasted with “حبّا,” grain among the foods God brings forth in the sequence begun at 80:24.
This continuation names grapes and green fodder, concrete produce in contrast to the section's dry thorn that does not nourish.
This continuation names olives and palms among the provisions that answer the section's failed food.
This continuation adds densely planted gardens to the food sequence, reversing the single useless thorn meal.
The section names a plant dry as thorn; this continuation names fruit and pasture, food-bearing growth rather than a meal that fails.
The section denies food's two functions; this sequence ends by calling its produce “متاعا لكم ولأنعامكم,” provision for people and livestock.
The section develops the dry-plant sense of ضريع; “فجعله غثاء أحوى” shows pasture becoming dark stubble, while leaving open the section's irony that this dried plant is imposed as food.
The section's food is a dry plant that cannot nourish; this crop scene says God could make what is sown “حطاما,” exposing how food production can fail.
The section labels جوع as hunger; here “الجوع” is one hardship in a test, a different frame from the section's punitive hunger that even food cannot relieve.
The section's “طعام” is a single thorny food that fails to nourish; here the Israelites ask for varied earth-grown foods instead of one food, distinguishing monotony from starvation.
The section identifies غ ن ي with sufficiency and lack of need; “فأغنى” names God making the needy Prophet free of want, opposite to food that “لا يغني” from hunger.
The section depicts people dependent on food that cannot feed them; this verse calls God the one who “يطعم ولا يطعم,” the provider who is not himself in need.
The section names غ ن ي as sufficiency and lack of need; this verse states that people are poor in need of God while God is “الغني,” marking the boundary between human hunger and divine sufficiency.

The section gives ضريع a secondary dictionary sense of thin drink and a sheep with a large udder; this Garden scene offers rivers of milk and honey, a specific image of drink and abundance opposite to the sparse failed meal.
After the section's cited full bellies in 37:66, this verse adds a mixture of boiling water over the Zaqqūm, completing the meal's punitive scene.
The section's cited meal belongs to a wider punishment scene; this neighbor says their return is to the blazing fire, locating the meal's outcome.
The section's quoted Zaqqūm comparison begins with “لآكلون من شجر من زقوم”; this verse identifies that tree as the food scene's source.
After the section's Zaqqūm and filled bellies, this verse adds drinking boiling water over it, extending failed food into harmful drink.
The section's named root جوع is hunger left unrelieved; here condemned people drink like thirsty camels, so ingestion does not end need.
The section's comparison to Zaqqūm is introduced here as “شجرة الزقوم,” identifying the tree behind the food of sinners.
The section's image of useless food becomes bodily torment here: the Zaqqūm mixture boils in the bellies.
This neighbor completes the section's Zaqqūm food scene by comparing the boiling in bellies to boiling hamim.
This precedes the section's cited exception in 78:25: the condemned “لا يذوقون فيها بردا ولا شرابا,” a no-relief pattern parallel to no food that eases hunger.
The section names ghislin as another exceptional Hell-food; this verse describes a drink of pus, another degraded intake rather than sustaining provision.
The section's food fails its purpose; this continuation says the pus is gulped with difficulty and brings death from every side, making ingestion itself affliction.
The section's dictionary description calls ضريع dried شبرق; this verse stages pasture being brought forth, the living growth before a plant dries.
After 56:65's crop made to crumble, this verse voices the growers' reaction; it continues the scene of food loss that makes need tangible.
This completes the crop-loss scene with “بل نحن محرومون”; it gives an explicit deprivation parallel to the section's food that leaves hunger unmet.
The section's dictionary gloss makes dryness central to ضريع; this parable shows vegetation becoming “هشيما” scattered by wind, a related scene of plant growth ending unusable.
The section identifies ضريع as a dried plant; this verse likewise follows vegetation from growth to yellowing and “حطاما,” making its dry-plant image a transience boundary.
The section links the ض ر ع family to severe need; this verse's “لعلهم يتضرعون” describes people driven by adversity to humble appeal, a response of need rather than sufficiency.
The section's dictionary sense of ضراعة is intense need; this verse repeats hardship leading people to “يضرعون,” making dependence audible as supplication.
The section labels the ض ر ع family with need and poverty; here people call on God “تضرعا وخفية” while seeking rescue at sea, an explicit appeal from helpless need.
